newsitem.title: USA: Mutual fund fees keep getting higher.
newsitem.headline: Mutual fund fees keep getting higher.

text.p: Do you know how much you are paying for your mutual fund? A lot more than you should be, according to Amy Arnott, editor of Morningstar Mutual Funds, a fund reporting service.
She argues that at a time when cash flowing into funds should offer investors some economies of scale, funds are "running the risk of pricing themselves out of business."

How? Arnott contends the management fees all funds charge are higher than they've ever been, despite the fact that fund managers are benefiting not only from economies of scale but from cheaper technology-based methods of sorting and selecting stocks.

A typical diversified stock fund created today can be expected to charge 0.72 percent of assets for management. That's about double the management fees charged by funds in the 1920s; a time, presumably, when stock data and good buys were harder to come by. Those management fees are in addition to the sales and advice charges you might be paying if you buy your funds through a broker or financial adviser.
Paradoxically, the increase in fund expenses is coming at a time when individual investors have cheaper and easier access to individual stocks than ever before.

Evergreen Enterprises, a Laurel, Md., firm that tracks individual stocks with discount buying plans, reports the number of companies that offer their shares directly to the public with no commissions whatsoever is pushing 100.
Most of the companies in the Standard & Poor's 500 also offer dividend reinvestment plans that allow individuals to keep buying more shares of companies they already own -- for no commissions.

Discount brokers, who charge reduced commissions and offer no investment advice, are competing largely on price these days, and telephone trades and online orders are cutting those commissions to rock-bottom levels.

It's against this backdrop that the funds are squeezing more and more out of their investors. Morningstar hypothesizes that an investor who pays a 1.5 percent commission to an adviser to select funds, and then another 1.5 percent management fee to the fund company itself, is cutting 3 percentage points of his or her return on the investment.

Coincidentally, or not so, that's about the amount by which a balanced mutual fund (which buys stocks and bonds) beats inflation over time. In other words, a balanced fund that cost you 3 percent theoretically wouldn't be any better than just keeping the money in Treasury bills over time.

Arnott overstates her case a bit: Most balanced funds don't have management fees that are quite that high, and if you make your own investment decisions and buy no-load stocks, you don't have to pay an adviser at all.

But her point is well taken. The quickest way to figure out what a management fee does to your return is to subtract it from your average annual return. If you're paying 0.75 percent of assets every year to stay in a fund that's returning 10 percent annually, that's like really earning 9.25 annually.
Invest $10,000 for 25 years, and that's a $17,000 difference. Not chicken feed.

But also not a horrible price to pay for the professional management, trading fees and services that come with a decent mutual fund. It's best to keep your eye on fund expenses without letting them make you crazy.
Morningstar lauds Vanguard and Twentieth Century for being the two fund companies that do their best to keep expenses down.

When you are selecting mutual funds, look for those that keep their expenses well below 1.5 percent, unless you have your own reasons for buying a fund that requires a lot of high-priced management. Even more important, look for fund companies that seem sincere about returning economies of scale to you.
